Tree appears to have initially developed as a phototropic leaner. Subsequent growth in the upper crown shows compensatory reaction growth trending more vertically. Epicormic shoots are present along the tension side consistent with this reaction growth pattern, reflecting the tree's adjustment to the earlier lean and a change in lighting conditions. While this information does not necessarily denote a defect, it does suggest a change in site conditions. A small rise in the ground surface was noticed beneath the ivy on the tension side, suggesting the presence of an old stump site within the structural root plate. The center of the presumed stump location is approximately 11 feet from the subject tree, suggesting a previously sheared or deformed structural root plate system. Soil resistance testing with a digital penetrometer (Newton measurements) indicated comparatively low soil resistance on the tension side (63.93 N and 121.7 N) near the historic stump location, while the compression side measured higher resistance (213 N and 300.7 N), indicating comparatively stronger soil support on the compression side. If the adjacent tree had remained intact and structurally sound, the subject tree’s lean alone may not present a concern; however, the historic removal, the elapsed time since that removal, and the relatively low soil resistance measured on the tension side suggest reduced soil support within that portion of the structural root plate.
